Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 111, verse 1:

Surat al-Masad

It is also called Surat al-Masad. It is Meccan, and its verses are five, without disagreement on either matter. When Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned before this the entry of people into the religion of Islam, He followed it with mention of the ruin of some who did not enter it and of their loss.

"Upon himself let him weep, whoever has wasted his life, and for him there is no share or portion of it."

Thus it has been said regarding the connection (ittisal) of this surah with what precedes. It has also been said that it is from the connection of threat with promise, and in each there is joy for him, upon him be prayers and peace. The Imam (al-Razi) said concerning this: when Allah, the Exalted, said, "To you is your religion, and to me is my religion" (Qur'an 109:6), it is as though the Prophet, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, said: "My Lord, what is my reward?" Allah, the Exalted, said: "For you is victory and conquest." He said: "What is the recompense of my uncle who called me to the worship of idols?" He said: "Perish the hands of Abu Lahab" (Qur'an 111:1). He placed the promise before the threat so that victory would be connected to His saying "and to me is my religion," and the threat would refer back to His saying "To you is your religion," in the manner of "On the Day when some faces will be bright" (Qur'an 3:106) and so on. So reflect on this harmony between these surahs, although Surat al-Nasr is among the last things revealed at Madinah, while Tabbat is among the first things revealed at Makkah, so that you may know that their arrangement is from Allah, the Exalted, and by His command.

Then he said: Another aspect is that when He said, "To you is your religion, and to me is my religion," it is as though it was said: "My Lord, what is the reward of the obedient one?" He said: The attainment of victory and conquest. Then it was said: "What is the reward of the disobedient one?" He said: Loss in this world and punishment in the Hereafter, as Surat Tabbat indicates. End. And it is as you see.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

"Tabbat" means: perished, as Ibn Jubayr and others said. From it is their saying: "Ashabbah am tabbah?" They mean: "Is she one who has grown old through decrepitude and incapacity, or one who is perished?" That is, she has lost, as Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar and Qatadah said. From the first (Ibn Jubayr) it is also reported: "she failed." And from Yaman ibn Thabit: "she was emptied of all good." These sayings, as in al-Bahr, are closely related in meaning.

Al-Shihab said: the root tabab revolves around cutting off, and this leads to ruin, which is why it was interpreted as such. Al-Raghib said: it is persistence in loss, and because it includes persistence it is said: "istatabba li-fulan kadha," meaning "it continued for so-and-so," and this meaning returns to ruin.

"The two hands of Abu Lahab." He is Abd al-Uzza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, the uncle of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, and he was extremely hostile and opposed to him, peace be upon him. Among that is what is in al-Majma' from Tariq al-Muharibi, who said: "While I was in the market of Dhu al-Majaz, suddenly there was a man young in age, saying: 'O people, say there is no god but Allah and you will prosper,' and behold, a man behind him was pelting him, having drawn blood from his shins and heels, and saying: 'O people, he is a liar, so do not believe him.' I said: 'Who is this?' They said: 'He is Muhammad, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, who claims he is a prophet, and this is his uncle Abu Lahab, who claims he is a liar.'"

Al-Imam Ahmad, al-Shaykhan and al-Tirmidhi reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When there was revealed, 'And warn your nearest kindred' (Qur'an 26:214), the Prophet, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, ascended al-Safa and began calling: 'O Banu Fihr! O Banu Adi!' for the clans of Quraysh, until they gathered. Whoever could not come out sent a messenger to see what it was. Abu Lahab came with Quraysh, and he said: 'Tell me, if I informed you that a cavalry in the valley intends to raid you, would you believe me?' They said: 'Yes; we have not tested you except as truthful.' He said: 'Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment.' Abu Lahab said: 'Perish you all day long! Did you gather us for this?' Then this (surah) was revealed."

It is also reported that, along with that saying, he took a stone in his hands to throw at the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him. From this is known the reason for choosing tabab over ruin and similar words mentioned earlier, and the attribution of it to his hands. Likewise, what al-Bayhaqi reported in al-Dala'il from Ibn Abbas, also: that Abu Lahab said when he came out of the defile (al-Shi'b) and supported Quraysh: "Muhammad promises us things that we do not see occurring; he claims they will occur after death." Then he placed something in his hands, then blew into his hands, then said: "Perish both of you! I see nothing in you of what Muhammad says." Then there was revealed: "Perish the two hands of Abu Lahab" (Qur'an 111:1).

From what is reported from Tariq the second (meaning) alone is known. The two hands are in their well-known sense, and the statement is an invocation for their ruin.

His saying, glory be to Him, "and he has perished" (wa tabba) is an invocation for the ruin of the whole of him. It is also permitted that both be informative, reporting the ruin of those two matters, and the use of the past tense in both places is to affirm the certainty of occurrence.

Al-Farra' said: the first is an invocation for the ruin of his whole person, on the basis that the two hands are either a metonymy for the self and the essence, because of the general connection between them, or a metaphor through the use of a part for the whole, as Muhyi al-Sunnah said. The response to this is that it is required that the whole be non-existent by the non-existence of the part; like the head, the neck and the hand, which are not so. This is not accepted, since leading scholars have stated otherwise here, and in His saying, "and do not cast yourselves with your own hands into destruction" (Qur'an 2:195). Or what is meant, as has been said, with that condition, is that the thing ceases to exist literally or legally, as in the use of "eye" for a lookout and "hand" for one who gives or who undertakes some actions; for the essence, insofar as it is characterized by what it is intended to be characterized by, ceases to exist by the non-existence of that organ. The second is a report of occurrence, that is: that happened and came to pass, like the saying of al-Nabighah:

"May Allah repay him with the worst of repayments for what he has done to me, the repayment of the snarling dogs, and he has done it."

It has been inferred that this clause is circumstantial (hali), with "qad" implied, according to the well-known view, as Ibn Mas'ud recited. In the two Sahihs and others, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas about the occasion of revelation: "Perish the two hands of Abu Lahab, and he has perished" (Qur'an 111:1). On this reading it is impossible for that to be an invocation, because "qad" does not enter upon verbs of supplication.

It was said: the first is a report about the ruin of his work, in that it did not benefit him nor avail him, since deeds are generally carried out by the hands. The second is a report about the ruin of himself.

In the interpretations, "the hand" means favour (ni'mah). He used to do good to the Prophet, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, and to Quraysh, and he would say: "If the matter belongs to Muhammad, I have a favour with him; and if it belongs to Quraysh, it is likewise." So it was declared that his hand which was with the Prophet, may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him, was lost through his enmity toward him, and his hand which was with Quraysh was also lost, by the loss of Quraysh and their ruin at the hand of the Prophet, peace be upon him. This is the meaning of "Perish the two hands of Abu Lahab."

The second is meant as a report of his own ruin, and he was mentioned by his kunya because he was known by it, and it is intended to publicize him with a curse of evil, and to remain a mark upon him; and mentioning him by the more famous of his two names is more fitting for this. This is supported by the reading of one who recited "yada Abu Lahab," as it is said: Ali ibn Abu Talib and Muawiyah ibn Abu Sufyan (recited it so), so that nothing of it would be changed, which would confuse the hearer; or from disliking the mention of his ugly name; or because, as was reported from Muqatil, he was called by that kunya for the blazing and brightness of his cheeks, so he was mentioned by it in mockery of him and of his pride in it; or for the paronomasia (tajnis) with dhat lahab, which corresponds to it in wording and meaning. The view that it is not a verbal paronomasia, because there is no confusion in the rhyme-ending, since they did not stipulate this in it; or that it is a metonymy for the one of Hellfire, so that it is as if it were said: "Perish the two hands of one of Hellfire." That is because his being attributed to the blaze, like the attribution of a father to a son, indicates his being connected to it and attached to it, as one says: "He is the father of goodness and the father of evil, and the brother of virtue and the brother of war," for one who is associated with and devoted to these matters. His constant association with that necessarily entails his being of Hellfire by customary implication, for the true blaze is the blaze of Jahannam. So the move from Abu Lahab to "one of Hellfire" is a move from the implicating to the implied, or the reverse, according to the two opinions on metonymy. For the connection between them in general is established in external reality and in the mind, except that this implication is only according to the first imposition, namely the idafi (genitival) one, and not the second, namely the proper-name one; and they consider in kunyas the original meanings. So Abu Lahab, by the proper-name imposition, is used for the specific person, and from him one passes, by his original imposition, to the one associated with and devoted to the blaze, and from him to the notion that he is of Hellfire. Thus it is a metonymy for the attribute through an intermediary. This is what the Second Allamah (al-Taftazani) chose: for him it is a metonymy without an intermediary, since its original meaning, namely the one associated with the blaze, is kept in view together with its proper-name meaning, and this is closer with the sign. For Abu Lahab is used for the specific person, and the speaker, on the basis of their consideration of original meanings in kunyas, moves from it to the original meaning, and then from it to the one of Hellfire, and its original meaning is not kept in view with it; otherwise the expression "Abu Lahab" in the verse would be a metaphor, whether its original meaning were kept in view with it by way of partiality or restriction, since it was not established for the whole. As for what has been said: that the literal meaning is not intended in a metonymy, and that the locus of benefit, truth and falsehood in it is the second meaning, and here the specific person is intended, this is nothing; for metonymy is an expression whose implied meaning is intended, while the literal meaning may also be intended with it, so both meanings may be intended here. In the Miftah there is an explicit statement that what is intended in a metonymy is the literal meaning and its implication together. Al-Sayyid also claimed that the metonymy in "Abu Lahab" is because he became famous by this name and by being of Hellfire, so that his name indicates that he is of Hellfire, like Hatim's indication that he is generous. So when it is uttered and intended to move to this meaning, it is a metonymy for it. But this has the objection that it would follow that metonymy in such a case would depend on the person's fame by that name, and this is not so, for people move from the kunya to what its named person necessarily implies by original consideration, without any dependence on fame. The poet said:

"I aimed at the excellences, that I might see him, out of a longing that nearly drew me to him;
so when I saw, I saw him unique, and I did not see among his sons one son beside him."

Yet in this there is much remoteness. Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn Kathir read "Abi Lahbin" with a sukun on the ha', and this is among the changes of proper names, as in al-Kashshaf. Abu al-Baqa' said: the fath and the sukun are two dialects, and this is analogical according to the Kufan school.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 111, verse 2:**

﴿What his wealth availed him not﴾. That is: his wealth did not avail him when destruction (tabab) befell him. This is on the basis that "ma" is a negation particle. It is also permissible that it be interrogative, in a position of nasb (accusative) governed by what follows it, as a direct object or an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq); that is: "What kind of availing, or what thing, did his wealth avail him?"

﴿And what he earned﴾. That is: and that which he earned, on the basis that "ma" is a relative pronoun (ma mawsulah). It is also permissible that it be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah); that is: and his earning. Abu Hayyan said: If the first "ma" is interrogative, then this one may also be interrogative; that is: "And what did he earn?"; that is: he did not earn anything. Issam al-Din said: It may be negative, and the meaning is: his wealth did not avail him against harm, and what he earned gave him no benefit. Its apparent sense is that he made the subject of "earned" (kasaba) the pronoun referring to wealth, and this, as you see, is far-fetched.

Al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's Al-Bahr al-Muhit) preferred that it be relative, with the returning pronoun omitted; that is: and that for which he had earnings from it: profits, outcomes, benefits, standing, and followers. Or: what his inherited wealth from his father availed him, and what he earned by himself, or his wealth and what he earned from his wicked deed, which is his scheming in enmity toward the Prophet (ﷺ), as al-Dahhak said; or from his deed which he thought would be of some use, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾, as Qatadah said.

From Ibn Abbas and Mujahid: "what he earned" refers to children. Abu Dawud related from A'ishah, traced to the Prophet: "Indeed the best of what a man eats is from his earnings, and indeed his child is from his earnings."

It is narrated that he used to say: "If what my nephew says is true, I will ransom myself from it with my wealth and my children." He had three sons: Utbah, Mu'attib, and Utaybah. Utbah and Mu'attib embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest (Fath), and the Prophet (ﷺ) rejoiced at their Islam and supplicated for them, and they witnessed Hunayn and al-Ta'if. Utaybah (diminutive) did not embrace Islam. Regarding this, the author of the book Al-Alibba' says:

I disliked Utaybah when he committed a crime, and I loved Utbah when he embraced Islam.
Likewise Mu'attib is a Muslim, so be cautious, and fear that you may revile a Muslim youth.

Umm Kulthum, the daughter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), was under Utaybah, and Ruqayyah, her sister, was under their brother Utbah. When this surah was revealed, Abu Lahab said to them: "My head and your heads are forbidden to one another unless you divorce the two daughters of Muhammad (ﷺ)." So they divorced them. However, Utaybah the diminutive had intended to go out to Syria with his father, so he said: "I will surely go to Muhammad (ﷺ) and harm him." He came to him and said: "O Muhammad, I disbelieve in the star when it sets, and in He who drew near and descended," then he spat toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but nothing afflicted him, peace be upon him. He also divorced his daughter Umm Kulthum, and so angered him, peace be upon him, by what he said and did. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O God, set against him one of Your dogs."

Abu Talib was present, disliked that, and said to him: "How self-sufficient you are, O nephew, from this supplication!" So he returned to his father, and then they set out for Syria. They halted at a stopping place, and a monk from a monastery looked down upon them and said to them: "This is a land full of beasts." Abu Lahab said: "Help me, O company of Quraysh, this night, for I fear for my son from the supplication of Muhammad (ﷺ)." So they gathered their camels and made them kneel around themselves out of fear of the lion. A lion came sniffing at their faces until it came to Utaybah and killed him. Regarding this, Hassan said:

Whoever returns this year to his family, the beast of prey does not consume the returnee.

Abu Lahab himself died of the plague ('adasah) seven nights after the Battle of Badr. His family shunned him for fear of contagion, for Quraysh used to guard against it as they would the plague. He remained three days until he stank. When they feared shame, they hired some Sudanese, who carried him and buried him. In another report: they dug a pit for him and pushed him in with a stick until he fell into it, then they pelted him with stones until they covered him. In yet another: they did not dig for him, but propped him against a wall and threw stones at him from behind until he was hidden. Thus the matter was as the Qur'an had foretold.

And Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read: "wa-ma iktasaba," with the taa of the iftiʻal form.

He will enter a Fire of blazing flame in the Hereafter, undoubtedly, and will suffer its heat. The sin (س) in "sayaslā" is for emphasizing the threat, and the tanwin in "nāran" is for magnification, meaning: a great fire.

"Dhāta lahab" (of blazing flame): possessing intense kindling and blazing. It is the Fire of Jahannam. The clause "mā aghnā" (his wealth did not avail him) and what follows: al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: it is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf) answering what he used to say: "I will ransom myself with my wealth," and what he imagined from his own sincerity. In it is a disgrace to him and a mockery of what he used to boast of, namely wealth and children. This clause depicts the destruction in a way that makes clear the failure of wealth and children to avail, and this is evident according to the interpretation of "what he earned" as referring to children. Some learned scholars said: the first (clause) refers to the destruction of his deeds, and this one refers to the destruction of his self. This also holds according to some of the previously mentioned aspects, so reflect and do not be heedless.

Al-Alusi's commentary on Surah 111 (al-Masad), verse 4:

Allah's saying, ﴿and his wife﴾, is a conjunction (ʿatf) on the pronoun hidden in ﴿will burn﴾, because of the separation by the object (al-fasl bi-l-mafʿul). His saying, ﴿carrying the firewood﴾, is in the accusative, given as a term of abuse and disparagement (ʿalā al-shatm wa-l-dhamm). It has also been said that it is in the accusative of circumstance (ʿalā al-ḥāliyya), on the basis that the construction (al-iḍāfa) is not a true one, because it refers to the future, as you will hear, God willing. She was Umm Jamil bint Harb, sister of Abu Sufyan.

Ibn ʿAsakir narrated from Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, from his father Muhammad al-Baqir, may Allah be pleased with them both, that ʿAqil ibn Abi Talib entered upon Muʿawiya, and Muʿawiya said to him: "Where do you think your uncle Abu Lahab is, in the Fire?" ʿAqil said to him: "When you enter it, he will be on your left, lying with your aunt, the firewood-carrier. And the rider is better than the one who is ridden."

I do not think this report from al-Sadiq is sound, because there is in it what there is (i.e., its faults), and she was, as is said in al-Bahr, cross-eyed (ʿawrāʾ). She was named this because, as Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Zayd, she used to bring thorny branches and cast them at night in the path of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. It was also said: she used to carry a bundle of thorns, colocynth and sadan (thistle), and scatter them at night on his path, peace be upon him, and the Messenger of Allah would step on them as one steps on silk. It is narrated from Qatada that, despite her great wealth, she used to carry firewood on her back out of extreme stinginess, and so she was reproached for stinginess.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him and from Mujahid that she used to walk about with slander (al-namima). Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it from al-Hasan. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Suddi, and it is said of one who goes about with it: "he carries firewood among the people", that is, he kindles strife among them (yūqid baynahum al-nāʾira) and stirs up evil (yu’ajjir al-sharr). Thus "firewood" is a metaphor (mustaʿār) for slander, and this is a well-known metaphor. From this is his saying:

*"From the white swords that were not drawn upon the back of a coat of mail, nor did she walk among the tribe with fresh firewood."*

He described it as fresh (raṭb) to indicate smoking (al-tadkhīn), which is an increase in evil, so there is in it a fine intensification (īghāl ḥasan). Likewise is the saying of the rajiz:

*"Truly the sons of al-Adram are firewood-carriers; they are the slanderers, in contentment and in anger."*

Ibn Jarir said: "carrier of sins and offences", from their saying: "So-and-so gathers firewood on his back" when he acquires sins and offences. The apparent view is that "firewood on her back" is a metaphor for sins, by the common factor that each of them is a source of burning. It has also been said: "al-ḥaṭab" is the plural of ḥāṭib, like ḥāris and ḥaras, meaning that she carries the wrongdoers to their crimes; but this is a distant interpretation.

Abu Haywa and Ibn Muqsim read: «sayuṣlā» with a damma on the yāʾ, a fatḥa on the ṣād and a shadda on the lām. And «wa-murayʾatuhu» with diminutive and hamza; and it was read «wa-muraytuhu» with diminutive, the hamza changed to yāʾ and assimilated.

Al-Hasan and Ibn Ishaq read «sayuṣlā» with a damma on the yāʾ and a sukun on the ṣād, and Abu ʿAmr elided the vowel of the hāʾ in «imraʾatuhu».

In another report, Abu Qilaba read: «ḥāmilata al-ḥaṭab» in the form fāʿila with an annexed genitive (muḍāfan). The majority read: «ḥammālatu al-ḥaṭab» with raf and idafa, and it was read «ḥammālatun li-l-ḥaṭab» with tanwin, in the nominative and accusative, and with the lam of genitive on al-ḥaṭab.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 111, verse 5 (part 1 of 3):**

The words of the Exalted, ﴿in her neck is a rope of palm-fiber﴾, form a sentence consisting of a fronted predicate and a delayed subject, in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in ﴿the firewood-carrier﴾. It has also been said that it relates to "his wife" (the noun in apposition, ma'ṭūf, to the pronoun). It has also been said that the prepositional phrase is a circumstantial clause relating to her, and "rope" (ḥabl) is raised by it as the agent (fā'il). It has also been said that the phrase is a predicate of "his wife," who is the subject (mubtada'), not in apposition to the pronoun, and "rope" is the agent.

On the reading "the firewood-carrier" in the nominative, it has been said that "his wife" is the subject and "the firewood-carrier" is the predicate. "In her neck is a rope" is a second predicate, or a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in ﴿the firewood-carrier﴾, or to the prepositional phrase in the same way. "Rope" is raised by it as the agent, or "his wife" is the subject and "the firewood-carrier" is its attribute, because it refers to the past, so it becomes definite through the annexation, and the predicate is as you have heard. Or "his wife" is in apposition to the pronoun, and "the firewood-carrier" is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: she is a firewood-carrier. What follows is a second predicate or a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in "the firewood-carrier," in the manner of what has passed. The construction admits other aspects of grammatical analysis (i'rab), which he will mention, God willing. Some of what we have stated here does not hold consistently across all the aspects of the meaning of the verse, as will be clear to the careful reflector upon examining them.

[Page 264]

*Al-masad* is that which has been twisted (musidda), that is, twisted tightly from ropes, made of the fiber of the doum palm, according to what Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) said, and from whatever fiber, according to what has been said. It has also been said that it is from the bark of a tree in Yemen called *al-masad*, and this was narrated from Ibn Zayd. It may also be, as in al-Bahr, from the hides of camels or their wool, and from this is his (the poet's) saying:

*"And a masad, twisted, of the she-camels, neither fangs nor incisors."*

That is: in her neck is a rope of what has been twisted from ropes. The intention is to depict her in the form of a woman who gathers firewood, carrying the bundle and tying it around her neck, as a debasement of her condition and a humiliation of her, so that she is mortified by this and her husband is mortified too, since they were in a house of honor and nobility and in a position of wealth and new prosperity. Some people reproached al-Fadl ibn al-Abbas ibn Utbah ibn Abi Lahab with "the firewood-carrier," so he said:

*"What do you want by reviling me and disparaging me, or by reproaching me with the firewood-carrier?*
*A noble lady, whose forehead is a blaze in glory, who was the offspring of an old man of ancient lineage."*

This angered her. It is related that when she heard the surah, she came to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), while he was with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the mosque, and in her hand was a stone (fihr). She said: "It has reached me that your companion has satirized me. By Allah, I will do such and such, and if he is a poet, then I am like him, I say:

*"We have disobeyed a blameworthy one (mudhammam), we have rejected him, his religion we have abandoned, and his command we have disobeyed."*

Allah made her sight blind to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It is related that Abu Bakr said to her: "Do you see anyone with me?" She said: "Do you mock me? I see no one but you." Abu Bakr was silent, and she departed, saying: "Quraysh knows that I am the daughter of its chief." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Angels screened him from her, so she did not see me, and Allah sufficed her evil."

It has been said that this is a supporting detail (tarshīḥ) for the metaphor, based on considering it in the sense of "the firewood-carrier." In al-Kashshaf: it may be that the meaning is: she will be in the fire of Hell in the form in which she was when she used to carry a bundle of thorns, so there will always be on her back a bundle of the firewood of the Fire from the tree of Zaqqum or from the *dari'* (thorny plant), and in her neck a rope of what has been twisted from the chains of the Fire, just as every criminal is punished with what is suited to his condition in his crime. On this interpretation, "rope" is used figuratively for "chain." This was narrated from Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid and Sufyan. As for the grammatical analysis according to al-Kashf: if "the firewood-carrier" is in the accusative, then it is a circumstantial clause, it and the sentence "in her neck is a rope," i.e. ﴿in her neck is a rope﴾, relating to the conjoined pronoun in ﴿she will burn﴾ (sayaṣlā), meaning: "his wife will burn in this state." Or "the firewood-carrier" is in the accusative by way of censure (dhamm), and the sentence alone is a circumstantial clause, or "his wife, in her neck is a rope" is a sentence that stands as a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun. It is possible to link one sentence to another sentence, though this is weak.

On the nominative reading, it is possible that the sentence is a circumstantial clause, and that "his wife" is in apposition to the subject (fā'il). "The firewood-carrier of the firewood, in her neck" is a sentence with no place in the grammatical structure, which serves as an explanation of the manner of her burning, meaning: she is the firewood-carrier. End. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

On all aspects and possibilities, the reason the Exalted did not say "in her throat" (*fī 'unuqihā*), though the usual practice is to mention the throat together with the shackle and the like which involve humiliation, as He said: ﴿upon their necks are shackles﴾, and the neck (*jīd*) together with ornaments, as in the saying of the poet:

*"Or more beautiful is the neck of the fair one, with its ornament."*

If He had said "her throat," it would have been a repugnant speech. In al-Rawd al-Anif, the author says: "Because it is a sarcasm, like ﴿so give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾, meaning: she has no neck to be adorned, and if she had one, this would be its ornament. And for the sake of belittling her, she is called 'his wife' and not 'his spouse' (zawj)." End.

This is very fine, but it is marred at its end by the Exalted's saying: ﴿and his wife standing﴾. Perhaps he relied here on the context for what he said. It is related from Qatadah that there was on her neck a necklace of *wadi'* (cowrie shells), and in its meaning is the saying of al-Hasan: "of beads." Ibn al-Musayyib said: it was a splendid necklace of jewels, and she said: "By al-Lat and al-Uzza, I will spend it on hostility to Muhammad (ﷺ)." Perhaps the meaning according to this is that in the Fire of Hell she will have a necklace of twisted iron in place of her necklace which she used to speak of:

[Page 265]

*"I will spend it..."* and so on.

According to what preceded, the disparagement of her necklace serves to emphasize her censure for stinginess, which is indicated by the Exalted's saying ﴿the firewood-carrier﴾, according to what we have quoted earlier from Qatadah, though it may admit other meanings. The reason for the use of "neck" in the sense mentioned is clear. Some have claimed that the words may be understood as a curse upon her with strangulation by a rope, and this is a far-fetched notion. It is mentioned that she died strangled by a rope with which she was carrying a bundle of firewood, but this does not require interpreting what was mentioned as a curse. This is what was raised as a difficulty regarding the obligation imposed on Abu Lahab to believe, together with the Exalted's saying ﴿he will burn﴾, etc.: that once Allah has informed about him that he will burn in the Fire, it is necessary that he will burn, and none will burn therein but the disbeliever, so the announcement of this includes the announcement that he will never believe. Therefore, when he was obligated to believe in what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought, and this is part of it, it follows that he was obligated to believe that he would not believe at all, which is a combination of contradictories, outside the bounds of possibility. It was answered that what he was obligated to believe is the belief in everything the Prophet (ﷺ) brought in general, not belief in the details of what the Noble Qur'an declares, so that it would follow that he is obligated to believe in his own continual non-belief. The same answer may be given regarding the obligation imposed on the disbelievers mentioned in the Exalted's saying: ﴿Say: O disbelievers...﴾, etc., to believe, based on their being specified, together with the Exalted's saying: ﴿nor will you worship what I worship﴾, etc., based on its indication of the continuation of their not worshipping what he (ﷺ) worships.

Some answered that the Exalted's saying ﴿he will burn﴾, etc., is not an explicit text that he will never believe at all, for burning in the Fire is not exclusive to disbelievers, so Abu Lahab may understand from it that his entry into the Fire is for his wickedness and sins, not for his disbelief. This does not apply to the answer regarding the obligation of those disbelievers, based on their understanding of the surah as indicating continuation. Another answered that whoever has been given such a statement and knows of it is obligated to believe in what else the Prophet (ﷺ) brought. Al-Ka'bi, Abu al-Husayn al-Basri, and likewise al-Qadi Abd al-Jabbar answered with something other than what was refuted by the Imam (al-Razi). It has been said, regarding this verse in particular, that the meaning is: he will burn in a fire of flame, and he will be eternal therein if he dies without believing, so this is not an explicit text that he will not believe. The implications of these answers and what is against them are to be sought in the lengthier books of the principles of jurisprudence and theology. It was used as evidence, from the Exalted's saying ﴿and his wife﴾, for the validity of the marriage contracts of disbelievers. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**Surah al-Ikhlas**

It is named so because of the monotheism (tawḥīd) it contains, and for this reason it is also called *al-Asās* (the Foundation), for monotheism is the root of all the roots of the religion. It is related from Ka'b, as the Hafiz Ibn Rajab said, that the seven heavens and the seven earths were founded upon this surah: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾. Al-Zamakhshari related it from Ubayy and Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), but none of the reliable hadith scholars mentioned it in this form. However that may be, what is meant by it, as he said, is that the heavens and the earths were created only to be signs of the oneness of Allah and knowledge of His attributes, which this surah comprises. It has been said that the meaning of its being founded upon it is that they were created only with truth, as He said: ﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them in play﴾ and ﴿We created them only with truth﴾, and the truth is justice and monotheism. This, if it does not return to the first meaning, is not free from scrutiny. It has also been said that what is meant is that the factor that validates their creation, after their essential possibility, is what this surah points to of the unity of the Mighty and Majestic, and the impossibility that He, glory be to Him, have a partner; for were it not so, their existence would not be possible, due to the possibility of mutual interference, as one of the eminent scholars explained in the proof-argument of the Exalted's saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been corrupted﴾. But there is remoteness in this.

It is also called the Surah of "Say: He is Allah, the One," as is well known, and the report also points to this. It is also called *al-Muqashqisha* (the Purifier), by what you have heard in the interpretation of the Surah of the Disbelievers; the Surah of Monotheism (tawḥīd); the Surah of Singling-out (tafrīd); the Surah of Stripping-bare (tajrīd); the Surah of Salvation (najāh); the Surah of Guardianship (wilāya); and the Surah of Knowledge (ma'rifa), because the knowledge of Allah is only complete by knowing what is in it.

There is a report that "a man prayed and recited it, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'This is a servant who knows his Lord.'"

It is called the Surah of Beauty (al-Jamāl), it has been said, because it is reported that he (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah is beautiful and loves beauty." They asked him (ﷺ) about this, and he said: "Ahad, Samad, He begets not nor is He begotten." I do not think the report is sound.

It is called the Surah of Lineage (al-Nisba), for it came as an answer to one who said: "Trace for us your Lord's lineage," as you will hear, God willing.

It has been said that it is called so because of what al-Tabarani narrated through the chain of Uthman ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Taraifi, from al-Wazi' ibn Nafi', from Abu Salamah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Everything has a lineage, and the lineage of Allah is: Say: He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Samad." It is, as the Hafiz Ibn Rajab said, very weak, and Uthman narrates the munkar (rejected) reports. In al-Mizan it is stated that it is fabricated (mawḍū').

It is called the Surah of the Samad, and the Surah of the Two Protectors (al-Mu'awwidhatān), because of what al-Nasa'i, al-Bazzar and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a sound chain, from Abdullah ibn Unays, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) placed his hand on my chest and said: "Say." I did not know what to say. Then he said: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾, and I said it until I finished it. Then he said: ﴿Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of the daybreak, from the evil of what He created﴾, and I said it until I finished it. Then he said: ﴿Say: I seek refuge with the Lord of mankind﴾, and I said it until I finished it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Thus seek refuge; the seekers of refuge have never sought refuge with the like of these, ever."

It is called the Surah of the Preventer (al-Māni'a). It has been said that this is because of what Ibn Abbas reported: "that when he (ﷺ) was taken up on the Night Journey, the Exalted said to His Prophet (ﷺ): 'I have given you the Surah of Sincerity (al-Ikhlas); it is among the treasures of the treasures of My Throne, and it is the Preventer: it prevents the anguishes of the grave and the breaths of the fires.'" The apparent view is that this report is not sound. It is contradicted by what Ibn al-Durays narrated from Abu Umamah: "Four verses were sent down from the treasure of the Throne, and none has been sent down from it other than these: the Mother of the Book, the Verse of the Throne, the closing verses of Surah al-Baqarah, and al-Kawthar."

The ruling on it is the ruling of the *marfu'* (a report traced back to the Prophet ﷺ, attributed to him directly). Indeed, Ibn Hibban, al-Daylami and others transmitted it with an *isnad* (chain of narration) from Abu Umamah, traced to the Prophet. As for Surat al-Mahdar, it is said that it is so named because the angels, upon them be peace, attend to listen to it when it is recited. As for Surat al-Munaffirah, it is said that it is so named because Satan flees (*yanfiru*) when it is recited. As for Surat al-Bara'ah, it is said: "Because of what is related, that he, upon him be blessings and peace, saw a man reciting it and said: 'As for this one, he has been cleared (*bari'a*) of shirk.'" I do not know who related that.

Yes, Abu Nu'aym related through 'Amr ibn Marzuq, from Shu'bah, from Muhajir, who said: "I heard a man say: I accompanied the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, on a journey, and he heard a man reciting ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾, and he said: 'He has been cleared of shirk.' And he heard another reciting ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾, and he said: 'He has been forgiven.'"

Accordingly, Surat al-Kafirun was attached to this name. Perhaps the better view is that it was so named because of what is in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi from Anas: "Whoever wishes to sleep on his bed and lies down on his right side, then recites ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ one hundred times, God the Exalted will record for him a release from the Fire."

[Surat] al-Mudhakkirah, because it reminds of pure monotheism (*tawhid*). Surat al-Nur: it is said that this is due to what is related from his saying, may God bless him and grant him peace: "Indeed, for everything there is a light, and the light of the Qur'an is ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾."

Surat al-Iman, because faith is not complete without what it includes of monotheism. Most of these names were mentioned by the Imam al-Razi, who explained the reason for naming them as he did. This man, may God have mercy on him, is not an imam in knowing the conditions of narrations; he does not distinguish the weak from the sound, or does not care about doing so, so he writes down whatever he came upon, even if he knows its extreme weakness.

It is Meccan according to the view of 'Abd Allah, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', Mujahid and Qatadah, and Medinan according to the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak; this was stated by [al-Andalusi] in *al-Bahr*.

The report of Ibn 'Abbas mentioned earlier, if it is authentic, is evident that in his view it is Meccan. In *al-Itqan* there are two views concerning it, due to two conflicting hadiths about the occasion of its revelation, and some reconciled between them by saying it was revealed more than once. Then it became clear to me that the preferred view is that it is Medinan. End of quote.

In light of what is in these two books, what al-Dawani said, that it is Meccan "by consensus", reflects, as is not hidden, a lack of wide reading. Its verses are five in the Meccan and Syrian counts, and four in other counts. It was placed here, it is said, for the sake of rhyme (*wizan*) between its endings and the ending of Surat al-Masad. It is also said, and this is the better view, that it is connected in meaning to ﴿Say: O you disbelievers﴾, so the two are like the statement of monotheism in negation and affirmation. For this reason, the two are called *al-Muqashqishatan* (the two that free from hypocrisy and disbelief). They are paired together in recitation in many prayers, as some of the imams stated: such as the two rak'ahs of the dawn prayer, the tawaf, the forenoon prayer, the sunnah of the maghrib, the dawn prayer of a traveler, and the maghrib prayer on Friday night. However, the two were separated by the two surahs for the reason mentioned earlier and similar reasons. And its being followed by Surat Tabbat, as a refutation of Abu Lahab specifically, is also relevant. Many reports have come concerning its excellence, among them what was mentioned just above.

[page 267]

Mubarak ibn Fadalah related from Anas that "a man said: O Messenger of God, I love this surah: ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾. He said: 'Your love for it has entered you into Paradise.'"

Imam Ahmad also transmitted it in *al-Musnad* from Abu al-Nadr, from the aforementioned Mubarak, from Anas. Al-Bukhari mentioned, as a suspended report (*ta'liq*), that love for it necessitates entry into Paradise.

Malik related from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, who said: "I heard Abu Hurayrah say: I came with the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and he heard a man reciting ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾, and the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'It is due (*wajabat*).' I said: What is due? He said: 'Paradise.'" It was transmitted by al-Nasa'i and al-Tirmidhi, who said: "A sound hadith which we only know from the hadith of Malik."

Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah and al-Tirmidhi transmitted, and al-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan gharib (fair and rare)," from Buraydah, that "the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, heard a man saying: 'I ask You, by my testifying that You are God, there is no god but You, the One, the Eternal Refuge, who has not begotten and was not begotten, and to whom no one is equal.' The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, he has asked God by His Greatest Name, that when He is called upon by it He responds, and when He is asked by it He gives.'"

In *al-Musnad* [it is related] from Mihjan ibn al-Adra' that "the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, entered the mosque and found a man who had finished his prayer and was reciting the tashahhud and saying: 'I ask You, O God, the One, the Unique, the Eternal Refuge, who has not begotten and was not begotten, and to whom no one is equal, that You forgive my sins, for You are the Forgiving, the Merciful.' The Prophet of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said three times: 'He has been forgiven, he has been forgiven, he has been forgiven.'"

Al-Bukhari, Malik, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i transmitted from Abu Sa'id that "a man heard another man reciting ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ repeatedly. When morning came, he went to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and mentioned that to him, and the man was belittling it. The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, it is truly equal to a third of the Qur'an.'"

Ahmad and al-Nasa'i in *al-Yawm wa al-Laylah* transmitted through Hushaym, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b or a man of the Ansar, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ has as it were recited a third of the Qur'an."

In the narration of Yusuf ibn 'Atiyyah al-Saffar with his chain, from Ubayy, traced to the Prophet: "Whoever recites ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ has as it were recited a third of the Qur'an, and there is recorded for him good deeds equal to the number of those who associated partners with God and believed in Him."

It has come that it is equal to a third of the Qur'an in several reports, both traced to the Prophet and stopping at a companion (*mawquf*).

In *al-Musnad*, through the chain of Ibn Lahi'ah, from al-Harith ibn Yazid, from Abu al-Haytham, from Abu Sa'id, who said: "Qatadah ibn al-Nu'man spent the whole night reciting ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾. This was mentioned to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and he said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, it is truly equal to half the Qur'an or a third of it.'"

This is taken as doubt on the part of the narrator, while the other reports specify a third. The meaning of this has been disputed. It is said: the meaning is that, in terms of its content, it is a third of the Qur'an when the Qur'an is divided into three parts, not that the reward for reciting it equals a third of the reward for the Qur'an. A group of scholars went to this view, but they differed in explaining it. It is said that the Qur'an includes stories and their rulings and beliefs, and all of these relate to beliefs, so it is a third in that respect. Al-Ghazali said in *al-Jawahir*, in summary: it is equivalent to a third of it in terms of the three kinds of knowledge that are the principles of what is in the Qur'an: the knowledge of the origin (God), the knowledge of the return (the afterlife), and the knowledge of what lies between them, that is, the straight path.

Al-Juwayni said: the subjects in the Qur'an are mostly the three principles by which Islam is valid and faith is attained: knowledge of God, acknowledgment of the truthfulness of His Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, and belief in standing before Him. This surah conveys the first principle, so it is a third of it in this respect. It is also said: the Qur'an has two parts: information and command, and information has two parts: information about the Creator and information about the created. These are three thirds, and Surat al-Ikhlas purified the information about the Creator, so it is a third in this respect. This, as you see, [is weak].

In any case, it has been said: there is no contradiction between the report of the third and the report of its being equal to the whole Qur'an, mentioned in *al-Kashshaf*, assuming it is established, because it may be said: it is equal to the Qur'an in the sense that the aim is monotheism, and everything else is a means to it. What supports considering the parts themselves, rather than the reward, is what is in Sahih Muslim through the chain of Qatadah, from Abu al-Darda', that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Is one of you unable to recite a third of the Qur'an every day?" They said: Yes. He said: "God has divided the Qur'an into three parts; ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ is a third of the Qur'an."

[page 268]

It is also said: the meaning is that it equals a third in reward, based on the apparent meaning of the hadiths. Ibn 'Aqil rejected this and said: it is not permissible that the meaning be "then he has the reward of a third of the Qur'an," because of his saying, may God bless him and grant him peace: "Whoever recites the Qur'an, for him there is ten good deeds for every letter."

So the reward for reciting the whole Qur'an would be multiplied many times over compared with the reward for reciting this surah. Al-Dawani raised this as a difficulty against this view and then answered it by saying that the reciter has two rewards: a detailed one according to the recitation of each letter, and a comprehensive one for completing the Qur'an. So the reward for ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ equals a third of the reward for the comprehensive completion, and no more. A parallel to this is when someone assigns a man who builds him a house to be paid dinars each day, and assigns to him, upon completing it, another reward besides his daily wage.

In al-Kirmani's commentary on al-Bukhari: "If you say: the hardship in reciting a third is greater than in reciting this surah, so how can its ruling be the same as it? I say: the reward for reciting a third is ten [times], and the reward for reciting this surah is equal to the reward for one recitation of it, because the comparison is in the basic reward, not the extra; and nine parts of it correspond to the increase in hardship."

Al-Khafaji, after saying: "There is nothing in what has been mentioned that soothes the heart and sets the mind at rest, and what I hold on this matter is that the one who contemplates the meaning of the speech of God, the Exalted, and reflects on His verses has a reward, and the one who recites it without understanding it has another reward. So the meaning is that whoever recites it observing the rights of its recitation, understanding its subtle meanings, his recitation of it with reflection and contemplation equals the reward of reciting a third of the Qur'an without considering its meanings; or [equals] a third which contains nothing related to knowledge of God and His unity. There is no wonder that, when the highest meanings are combined with some of the noblest words, it equals in value, of the same kind as those words, a large amount, like a gold plate weighing ten mithqals inlaid with the finest jewels, which is worth a thousand mithqals of gold or more." End of quote. I do not see in it much distinction over what was mentioned before.

What I choose is to say: there is no barrier to God, Mighty and Majestic, specifying some acts of worship that involve little hardship with a reward greater than the reward of their kind that are more difficult, by manifold multiples. He, glorified be He, is the One whom no one can restrain, whose generosity and bounty know no end, so it is not far-fetched that He, exalted is He, bestow upon the reciter of the Qur'an a good deed for every letter, and increase beyond that manifold for the reciter of Surat al-Ikhlas, such that its reward equals the reward of the reciter of a third of it that does not include that surah. He entrusts the wisdom of the specification to His knowledge, glorified be He, and the same is said of similar cases. This is what is meant by those who made it part of the ambiguous matters (*mutashabih*) whose knowledge God has reserved for Himself. This is no more remote or unprecedented than specifying some times and places, which are identical in essence, by saying that worship in them, even if little, has a reward that is manifold greater than the worship in a neighboring place, even if much. Indeed, He, glorified be He, has specified some times and places with the obligation of worship in them, and some with their prohibition, and He has in all of that wisdoms of which He alone is most aware.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: silence on this question is better than speech about it and safer. Likewise the hadith of Mu'awiyah ibn Mu'awiyah al-Laythi with which the Imam opened the discussion of this noble surah, which al-Tabarani and Abu Ya'la transmitted through chains that are all weak; and the authentic hadiths concerning it are sufficient to show its excellence. Indeed,

[page 269]

It was said regarding this: it is the best surah in the Qur'an. Some of those who held this view cited what al-Darimi narrated in his Musnad from Abu al-Mughira, from Safwan al-Kala'i, who said: "A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, which of the surahs of the Qur'an is greatest?' He said: 'Say: He is Allah, the One (Qul huwa Allahu ahad).'"

And in the Musnad, through two chains, that of Mu'adh ibn Rifa'a and that of Usayd ibn Abd al-Rahman, from Uqba ibn Amir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Shall I not teach you the best three surahs that were revealed in the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the Great Qur'an?' I said: 'Yes.' He then recited to me: Say: He is Allah, the One; Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak; and Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind. Then he said: 'O Uqba, do not forget them, and do not spend a night without reciting them.'"

Al-Tirmidhi narrated part of this hadith and graded it hasan. However, it does not indicate that it is the best of the surahs of the Qur'an absolutely, but rather that it is among the best.

Ibn al-Hassad said: "It is strange that someone would deny the difference in merit, given the abundance of texts about it." Those who affirmed preference differed. Some of them said: the excellence returns to the magnitude and multiplication of reward according to the movements of the soul, its fear and its contemplation when encountering the descriptions of exaltedness. It was also said: rather, it returns to the wording itself; for what the Surah al-Ikhlas, for example, contains of the indication of Divine Oneness and His attributes is not present in "Tabbat" (Surah al-Masad), for example. So the preference lies in the wondrous meanings and their abundance.

Al-Halimi related from al-Bayhaqi that the meaning of preference among verses and surahs returns to several things. The first is that acting upon it is better than acting upon another and more beneficial to people. On this basis, it is said that verses of command and prohibition, and of promise and threat, are better than verses of narrative; because they are intended to emphasize command, prohibition, warning and glad tidings, and people have no independence from these matters, whereas they may dispense with narratives. Therefore, what is more beneficial and useful for them, of that which serves as foundations, is better for them than what is made subordinate to what is necessary.

The second is that it may be said: the verses that include the enumeration of Allah's names, the explanation of His attributes, and the indication of His greatness, Exalted is He, are superior, in the sense that they are more sublime and greater in standing than those that do not include that.

The third is that it may be said: one surah is better than another surah, or one verse is better than another verse, in the sense that the reciter gains from reciting it a benefit in this world besides the deferred reward, and through reciting it he fulfills an act of worship, such as the Verse of the Throne, Surat al-Ikhlas, and the two Mu'awwidhatayn. For its reciter hastens, by reciting it, to guard against what he fears and to seek protection in Allah, Exalted is He; and through its recitation he fulfills the worship of Allah, glory be to Him, because it contains the remembrance of Him, Exalted is He, through the lofty attributes, in the manner of belief in them and the tranquility of the soul in the excellence of that remembrance and its blessing. As for verses of wisdom, the mere recitation of them does not establish a ruling; rather, through them knowledge is attained.

It may also be said that one surah is better than another because Allah, Exalted is He, made its recitation equal to the recitation of many times its like of other surahs, and made for it a reward which He did not make for others, even though the meaning for which it attained this measure does not appear to us. This is analogous to what is said regarding the preference of times and places over one another, as you have just heard. In sum, preference according to any of these considerations does not conflict with all of it being the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and of equal relation to Him, glory be to Him, as is not hidden. And Allah knows best.
